article.articleHeadline: 175 Indonesian National Armed Forces soldiers dispatched to the Congo; there is an Ebola threat in the zone of operations that must be monitored - Jakarta Zone.
article.articleSummary: 175 Indonesian National Armed Forces soldiers from three branches were deployed on 17 July 2026 to the Democratic Republic of the Congo for the United Nations MONUSCO peacekeeping mission. The departure ceremony occurred at Lapangan Prima, TNI Headquarters, Jakarta, with Panglima TNI General Agus Subiyanto represented by Asisten Operasi Letjen Bobby Rinal Makmun. The contingent, Satgas Kizi TNI Konga XX-W, is a Kompi Zeni (engineer company) focusing on construction, maintenance, repair, and technical support rather than direct combat. In the field, they will undertake infrastructure projects to enable MONUSCO operations. The mission contends with armed conflict and Ebola risk in parts of the Congo, prompting explicit orders to enforce strict health protocols and uphold safety, quality, and accountability. Output from their work is expected to influence overall mission effectiveness in a demanding operational zone with limited infrastructure.

article.articleHeadline: Supporting surveillance and response priorities for the 2026 DRC Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak -- Tshopo cohort, Rapid Release (17 July 2026)
article.articleSummary: Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) centers on Kisangani, Tshopo Province, as a high-connectivity mobility hub for surveillance. A rapid release using anonymised mobile operator data from three Kisangani health zones (up to 8 June 2026) shows strong links to Kinshasa and Congo River river-port towns, with notable connectivity to Ituri, Maniema, Nord-Kivu, Bas-Uele, and Haut-Uele, and lesser ties to Lubumbashi/Haut-Katanga. As of 13 July 2026, there are 4 confirmed Ebola Bundibugyo cases in Tshopo, underscoring cross-regional transmission risk. The report cautions about cross-border spread toward the Republic of Congo via Congo River border sites, and notes Bondo HZ in Bas-Uele with crossings to CAR. Among top 50 connected health zones, 15 are in Kinshasa province, emphasizing urban importation risk and the need for prioritized surveillance and response in mobile-healthy regions.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Ivory Coast: "No case detected on the territory," reassures the Director General of the INHP.
article.articleSummary: Ivory Coast reports no Ebola virus cases on its territory as of July 20, 2026, according to INHP Director-General Prof. Ekra Kouadio Daniel. While an Ebola outbreak is ongoing in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri province) since mid-May, with spread to neighboring Uganda, Ivory Coast has established a surveillance and detection system to prevent importation. The main objective is early detection. At Félix Houphouët-Boigny International Airport, temperature screening via thermal cameras, hand sanitizer, and rapid isolation/quarantine arrangements are in place; land borders also have temperature checks and hygiene stations, with training for regional and local health authorities to ensure rapid case management. The INHP coordinates surveillance through an Emergency Health Operations Center; Côte d’Ivoire can identify the Ebola virus type in circulation. Diagnostic kits are provided by the Pasteur Institute, with WHO collaboration providing information and training.

article.articleHeadline: Kwilu: Malaria has killed 146 people in six months, the disease henceforth.
article.articleSummary: Malaria outbreak in Kwilu province has caused 146 deaths among 387,874 cases in the first six months of the year, with all 24 health zones affected and both uncomplicated and severe forms reported, according to provincial Health Minister Robert Dinsodi. The village of Mukulubiala in Bulungu territory emerged as a critical hot-spot, where a June surge produced fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, yielding about ten deaths in a matter of days. Emergency field teams have stabilized the Bulungu sector, and Mukulubiala records 72 cases and 15 deaths (8 women, 7 men) to date, with no new cases or deaths since direct medical intervention began. Samples—5 water, 30 blood, 28 salt—have been sent to Kinshasa’s INRB for analysis to exclude other etiologies; results are pending. Authorities call for expanded distribution of insecticide-treated nets and anti-malarial inputs as the outbreak persists across Kwilu.

article.articleHeadline: Congo-Ebola: Community Leaders Trained to Strengthen Prevention.
article.articleSummary: Community leaders in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, were trained on July 17 to strengthen vigilance and response to Ebola virus threats. Participants learned transmission modes, warning signs, preventive measures, and procedures for suspected cases, with emphasis on rapid reporting to health authorities and disseminating best practices within communities. The action reflects regional health strengthening and ongoing preparedness to prevent Ebola's introduction into the Republic of Congo amid cross-border risk. No case counts were reported in the article.

article.articleHeadline: A virus dormant for 14 years suddenly awakens, killing 828 people in two months.
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus has caused 828 deaths and 377 recoveries after awakening from a 14-year dormancy, with ongoing transmission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and related regional concerns. There is no approved antiviral; care is entirely supportive (fluids, oxygen, nutrition) and includes treating coinfections such as malaria and typhoid to maintain body function while the immune system responds. Three therapies show promise: MBP134, a pan-ebolavirus bispecific antibody targeting two sites on the surface glycoprotein (active against Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses); maftivimab, a monoclonal antibody prioritized by WHO but not yet in trials; and remdesivir, a broad-spectrum RNA polymerase inhibitor. In June, Uganda received over 2,000 remdesivir vials. The PARTNERS trial in the DRC began July 2, randomizing confirmed cases to four arms (supportive care alone; plus MBP134; plus remdesivir; or plus both MBP134 and remdesivir) aiming 700–1,000 participants over six months. July 14 launched obeldesivir (oral remdesivir prodrug) trials with donations of 2,400 obeldesivir and 2,000 remdesivir. Xylomed of South Africa plans 3B trials in DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan for an oral small-molecule inhibitor, potentially usable at home for children over two.

article.articleHeadline: AI and climate alerts, massacre in Honduras, Ebola, and migrant women... Friday's news.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, is being stretched by population movement, with the IOM reporting seven million checks and more than 200 points monitored for cross-provincial movement. Authorities say over 50 bodies have been moved between provinces, districts and health zones, all Ebola-positive, though none crossed international borders. WHO notes families try to repatriate bodies for burial, complicating containment. In Honduras, a United Nations special rapporteur calls for independent investigation into the May 21 mass killing of 20 campesinos near Rigores, Bajo Aguán, including 14 men, 3 women and 3 minors aged 14, 14 and 17, urging accountability and reparations. Separately, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres says AI can expand early warnings for floods, storms, fires, and droughts, but vulnerable nations lacking meteorological stations must receive technology and training; system coverage stands at 128 countries, with calls for renewable energy powering data centers by 2030.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Bunia: an information kiosk installed in the city center to counter rumors - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease in Bunia, Ituri province, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, is being addressed with an information kiosk in Bunia’s city center to counter rumors and improve outbreak response. article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Strengthened awareness campaigns within the Archdiocese of Kisangani - ACP
article.articleSummary: Ebola awareness campaigns have been strengthened in the Archdiocese of Kisangani, in Tshopo Province, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Through the diocesan Office of Medical Works, the archbishop’s pastoral letter is read each Sunday in parishes to warn the faithful and urge adherence to barrier measures. Besides handwashing kits at church entrances, priests read the message during Eucharist to reinforce prevention. Masks remain insuffciently used. Other denominations, including Protestant and revival churches, are also mobilizing, with handwashing devices installed at some worship sites, though challenges remain in teaching Sunday school children and maintaining physical distancing. In large congregations such as Cité de Refuge and Hebron, no visible prevention measures were observed. Ebola cases with deaths have been recorded in the area, though exact numbers are not provided. The public health message stresses taking Ebola seriously and following authorities’ sanitary guidelines.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: in Djugu, nine health posts out of twelve have closed their doors.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo worsens in Djugu, Ituri, with 2,344 cases and 930 deaths reported as of 18 July; Ituri now has 27 of 36 health zones affected. In Limani's Héritage health area, nine of twelve health posts have closed, crowding the few remaining facilities. On 15 July, local leaders warned the situation is grave, with over a hundred deaths reported locally, though officials have not confirmed these provisional figures. Denial of preventive measures by communities in Djatsi and Pitsi—parallels observed north in Haut-Uele—fuel transmission. Kinshasa reported on 16 July that all suspected cases are tested and diagnoses provided within 24 hours by INRB, yet this requires functioning clinics. Limani’s closures impede screening, isolation, and supportive care for Bundibugyo, the Ebola strain there, for which no vaccine or specific treatment exists.

article.articleHeadline: Equatorial Guinea: an Ebola alert at the hotel where Washington is deporting migrants.
article.articleSummary: An Ebola alert centers on a Malabo hotel in Equatorial Guinea where 17 migrants deported from the United States are being held under a government detention program. Lawyers and two anonymous deportees allege that a man, then a woman, were brought to the hotel by medical staff in protective gear and placed on a floor below detainees; a doctor allegedly told them in English that they were suspected Ebola cases. No health authority—Ministry of Health, WHO, or Africa CDC—has confirmed or denied the claim, and Equatorial Guinea is not listed in current outbreak bulletins. The Associated Press has seen footage of staff transporting patients to the hotel, which previously functioned as a Covid-19 isolation site. The 17 detainees (four women, 13 men) originate from Angola, Mauritania, and Ethiopia, detained since October 2025 under a US deportation agreement worth about $7.5 million. Context notes a Congo outbreak (Bundibugyo strain) with thousands of cases in the DRC, but no confirmed link to Equatorial Guinea.

The group will use Citizen Voice Lab channels and social media—Facebook, WhatsApp, X, TikTok, YouTube—to disseminate reliable information and promote responsible civic dialogue. They also vowed to mobilize youth for awareness, alerts, and protection, declaring that a responsible, connected, engaged youth is a bulwark against Ebola.

article.articleHeadline: 'Ambulant Ebola': why the Congo outbreak is so hard to contain.
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus (Bundibugyo strain) drives an 'ambulant Ebola' pattern in the Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak, where patients become ill enough to transmit the virus but remain mobile, facilitating community spread. Virologist Corri Levine, whose PhD work focused on Bundibugyo, observed that this strain replicates more slowly than Zaire ebolavirus, the lineage behind the West Africa epidemic a decade earlier. The slower disease progression means symptoms may be present without disabling illness, creating a longer window for detection and intervention. Early antiviral treatment offers a better chance of altering outcomes before viral loads reach septic shock and multi-organ failure. Levine’s insights come from laboratory work at the University of Texas Medical Branch in a BSL-4 facility, underscoring that earlier, timely treatment could improve survival and help curb transmission in the Congo outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Uganda's positive response restores hope for Kasindi traders - ACP.
article.articleSummary: As of 20 July 2026, Ebola outbreak in Uganda drives cautious optimism for cross-border trade between Kasindi, Nord-Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Mpondwe, Uganda, as Uganda's epidemiological situation shows signs of improvement. Traders told ACP on Monday that activity could restart across the Kasindi–Mpondwe frontier, previously closed, sharply constraining commerce. Fabrice Nzanzu Ndavo, head of the Comesa cross-border trade information desk at Kasindi, cited improving epidemiology in neighboring Uganda as a key factor for resuming cross-border commerce. Since the frontier closure, staple foods such as bananas and tomatoes failed to reach markets, worsening living standards on both sides. Prices at Kasindi surged. Traders had faced uncertainty until Uganda reported the last confirmed Ebola case and subsequent suspected cases, reviving hope for reopening. Kasindi and Mpondwe economies rely predominantly on cross-border trade.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: the National Institute of Biomedical Research bets on rapid tests (Professor Muyembe) - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease (EVD) response in the Democratic Republic of Congo centers on rapid diagnostic tests, according to INRB Director-General Professor Jean-Jacques Muyembe in Kinshasa on July 20, 2026. The institute prioritizes field evaluation of rapid tests received from various pharmaceutical firms to determine suitability for use in Ituri and other provinces. A second priority focuses on understanding transmission dynamics, with emphasis on healthcare workers, health facilities, and gold mining employers of those working in Mongbwalu. A third priority seeks to elucidate the pathophysiology of EVD through localized anatomopathological studies across different organs. An international study will evaluate the Ebola vaccine before deployment in collaboration with partners to characterize differences among circulating strains. Muyembe also said Kinshasa has not recorded any positive case yet, and reinforced barrier measures such as handwashing and avoiding contact with contaminated individuals. Additional projects will be funded as the response evolves.

article.articleHeadline: The Ebola strain circulating in Africa is genetically different from the viruses of past epidemics.
article.articleSummary: Ebola in Africa is caused by the Bundibugyo variant recently analyzed by scientists from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and other countries. The circulating strain differs significantly from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, with about 1.1% genome divergence. The Ugandan sequence carried 219 single-nucleotide variations, signaling a new evolutionary branch rather than a wholly new virus. Mutations appear in glycoprotein, polymerase, and other proteins involved in replication and immune suppression; these changes could affect cell entry, replication, or immune evasion, but a single genome sequence cannot confirm higher transmissibility or virulence without further cellular, animal, and clinical data. In the current Congo outbreak, 2,344 people have been infected and 930 have died, yielding a case fatality of about 39.7%. There is no specific therapy for Bundibyo Ebola yet, while vaccine efforts are discussed in related reports.

article.articleHeadline: Frontline Observations on Disaster Prevention, Mitigation, and Relief | A Day in the Life of Local CDC Personnel in Disaster Areas
article.articleSummary: Flood-response operations in Guangxi’s Hengzhou (a district under Nanning City) mobilized over 500 personnel from the Nanning CDC to three flood-affected areas: Hengzhou, Yunbiao Town, and Bin Yang Gantang, to conduct post-disaster sanitation and disease prevention. On July 18, teams moved by foot along mud-laden roads to Dengxu Village and Wangbaotun, delivering disinfection spray and health education to about 140 households. They emphasized simple, correct mixing of chlorine disinfectants (one cap concentrate to one cap water) and wearing gloves and masks due to irritant disinfectants. Health education extended to village cadres to multiply reach. Officials warned that 7–15 days after flooding is a high-risk window for intestinal, respiratory, and vector-borne diseases; in addition to spraying, authorities will conduct mosquito/larval control and follow-up sanitation until all affected households are covered, then return to Nanning.

article.articleHeadline: New complication of COVID-19 infection identified in recovered patients.
article.articleSummary: Recovered COVID-19 patients are reported to have a new complication: eye nerve damage, including reduced corneal nerve fiber density and impaired pupil light reflex, cited in international medical journals. The condition may be missed in routine ophthalmologic exams, yet sufferers may experience years of photophobia, rapid eye fatigue, blurred vision, headaches, and computer-work discomfort. The study sample was small, leaving prevalence unknown and no proven treatment currently. Context: COVID-19 emerged in Wuhan in December 2019; WHO declared a pandemic in March 2020. In Russia, as of July 20, 2026, there have been 23,014,969 confirmed cases, 22,458,308 recoveries, 400,023 deaths; 156,638 active cases, with none in critical condition.

article.articleHeadline: What Is Brucellosis? How to Prevent It? The Full Explanation in One Go.
article.articleSummary: Brucellosis, a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella bacteria, is a Category B infectious disease under China’s Law on the Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases. Primary sources are livestock, especially sheep, goats, and cattle; other animals such as pigs, camels, dogs, horses, deer, and yaks may carry Brucella. High‑risk groups include veterinarians, herders, livestock handlers, slaughterhouse workers, milking staff, fur and meat processors, and veterinary inspectors; general exposure to contaminated animals or dairy/meat products also poses risk. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected animals or contaminated environments (skin/mucous membranes), ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products or undercooked meat, and inhalation of contaminated aerosols in abattoirs or fur facilities. Incubation is 1–4 weeks; early symptoms are non-specific, with fever, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, headaches, and musculoskeletal pain; untreated cases can become chronic. Prevention emphasizes PPE, hygiene, thorough cooking, avoiding raw dairy and cross-contamination; human-to-human transmission is extremely rare. Beijing CDC.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquito control measures to be carried out around Wynn Macau after guest with dengue fever recently stayed

Dengue virus transmission occurs via bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes and is not transmitted directly between people; a mosquito that bites a dengue patient remains infectious for life. The initiative aims to reduce local mosquito populations and transmission risk in the hotel vicinity.

article.articleHeadline: Ex-servicemen’s disease case: two community transmissions recorded in the past week.
article.articleSummary: Two community-acquired cases of Legionnaires’ disease were identified in Hong Kong between July 12 and 18, 2026. A 67-year-old man from Kowloon City and a 69-year-old woman from the Central and Western District, both with chronic illnesses, were confirmed as part of the Centre for Health Protection’s ongoing surveillance. Epidemiological investigations are under way to determine infection sources and high-risk exposures, with preliminary findings indicating sporadic cases not linked to earlier local cases. As of July 20, 2026, Hong Kong has recorded 95 Legionnaires’ disease cases this year; 2025 saw 167 cases and 2024 had 135. The CHP notes Legionella bacteria can survive in various water environments, including cooling towers, underscoring environmental tracing needs. No evidence of imported or exported case connections is reported.

article.articleHeadline: Spent a fortune on a blind date and a shotgun wedding! The pregnancy test report stuns the husband—the wife is a drug addict who has served time and even contracted syphilis.
article.articleSummary: From Jiangxi Province, China, a man traveled to Guiyang, Guizhou Province, through a matchmaking intermediary and quickly married, spending over 300,000 yuan. Prenatal health screening revealed the wife concealed a history of drug use, involvement in a money-laundering case, and prior imprisonment, and she tested positive for syphilis. The premarital medical report is suspected to be forged, prompting the family to allege that the matchmaking agency and bride hid crucial facts, causing marriage registration without full disclosure. Following the discovery, the husband sought to recover costs and hold those responsible; the pursuit has lasted more than six months with no recovery yet. Local authorities have formed a dedicated task force to investigate potential matchmaking fraud, forged documents, and other violations to protect citizens.

article.articleSummary: CBP planned to question Peter Daszak, EcoHealth Alliance chief, on his Feb. 5, 2021 return from the WHO SARS‑CoV‑2 origins investigation at JFK, labeling him a 'high person of interest' due to 15+ years of collaboration with the Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV), ties to its lead researcher Zhengli Shi, and NIH funding for bat coronavirus research. NIH reportedly asked Daszak to retrieve the original WIV type specimen for genetic analysis and return it to the United States, and to explain aspects of his collaboration, including related cell phone data. CBP considered operations in China and contact checks at WIV to assess potential illegal samples. Three days before arrival, the FBI New York Field Office requested halting the stop, so the inspection never occurred. The records reflect interagency disagreement over the investigation into COVID-19 origins and concerns about conflicts of interest.

article.articleHeadline: Dien Bien Department of Health safeguards the environment, preventing malaria from returning.
article.articleSummary: Malaria elimination is being safeguarded in Dien Bien Province, Vietnam, to prevent resurgence. From 2022 through 2025 the province reported zero new malaria cases, including domestic and imported infections. On 30 June 2025, the Central Institute of Malariology, Parasitology and Entomology issued Decision 685/QĐ-VSR recognizing Dien Bien as malaria-eliminated, marking a shift to maintenance, surveillance, and prevention of reintroduction. A 16 July conference mobilized resources for ongoing control, and the RA I4E project (2024–2026) will be implemented in Muong Toong, Muong Nhe, and Dien Bien Phu Ward. Key actions include sustaining microscopic networks to detect cases; providing monthly travel subsidies for 14 village health workers in hotspot areas; strengthening epidemiological surveillance from provincial to commune levels; and ensuring drug supply, rapid tests, insecticide-treated nets, and treated hammocks. Sustained local-government and community engagement remains crucial.

article.articleHeadline: The Whole Family Infected with Dog and Cat Parasites.
article.articleSummary: July 20, 2026, Hanoi, Vietnam – A family of three (Lan, 38; husband 42; daughter 9) presented with fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and intermittent itching. They have kept a cat for eight years. Tests confirmed Toxocara infection (roundworms) with eosinophilia and positive stool tests. Dr. Le Xuan Luat notes that close contact with pets—especially sharing a bed—without routine deworming and good hygiene increases exposure risk. Toxocara eggs shed by dogs and cats contaminate soil, dust, surfaces, and fur; humans acquire infection by ingesting eggs and may be asymptomatic or have fatigue, abdominal pain, digestive disturbance, and itching, with larvae potentially migrating to liver, lungs, or eyes causing organ damage. The family was treated and stable after three months; they will keep the cat but deworm pets regularly, clean living areas, wash hands, and avoid cats sleeping on the bed. Other pet-linked risks include fungal infections, Bartonella cat scratch disease, and rabies.

article.articleHeadline: Lam Dong Province tightens prevention and control of hand-foot-mouth disease after two deaths from EV71 virus infection
article.articleSummary: Lam Dong Province, Vietnam reports 3,072 hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD) cases through July 2026, up from 2025, with two Enterovirus 71 (EV71)–related deaths in Ta Nang commune. Investigations link fatalities to delayed detection, monitoring gaps, and late treatment, with caregivers failing to recognize warning signs or relying on non-inpatient care. The provincial Department of Health will mobilize the Center for Disease Control to form rapid response teams, support outbreak investigations, and implement control measures. Community outreach will be intensified, especially in ethnic minority areas, engaging local authorities, trusted community figures, religious leaders, and organizations to promote early recognition and timely hospital referral. All health facilities, including private clinics, must enforce strict triage and treatment protocols to avoid emergency delays. A door-to-door survey will identify hidden cases; inspections of kindergartens and private centers will suspend facilities not meeting hygiene standards. Ta Nang will receive intensified supervision, distribution of Cloramin B, and home hygiene guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Five-day fever, a 2-year-old girl survived septic shock thanks to detection of a mosquito bite mark.
article.articleSummary: A 24-month-old girl from Lao Cai, Vietnam, survived septic shock due to scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) after five days of fever and a day of diarrhea. On admission to Hai Phong National Pediatric Hospital, she was lethargic with signs of severe infection; a abdominal eschar—a classic diagnostic clue for scrub typhus—was identified. She required aggressive critical care, including endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, central venous catheter, vasopressors, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. After 24 hours vasopressors were withdrawn, after 3 days she was weaned from ventilation, and after 11 days of intensive care she was stabilized and discharged. Scrub typhus is transmitted by chigger mite bites in areas with dense vegetation and can rapidly progress to multi-organ dysfunction if not promptly treated. Thorough full-body examination for eschars is essential to guide timely therapy and prevent mortality.

article.articleHeadline: Rio Branco accounts for 61% of confirmed dengue cases in Acre in 2026.
article.articleSummary: Rio Branco remains the dengue epicenter in Acre, Brazil, with 607 of 993 confirmed cases (61.1%) through weeks 1–20 of 2026. The state totals 1,455 probable dengue notifications, with 993 confirmed. Despite an 84.5% drop in positive diagnoses from 2025 (6,407 cases that year), the incidence is 165.2 per 100,000, indicating active transmission. By region, the Lower Acre Region accounts for 660 confirmed cases (66.5%), led by Rio Branco and Sena Madureira (19). The Juruá Region has 266 cases (26.8%), concentrated in Cruzeiro do Sul (153) and Mâncio Lima (66). The Alto Acre Region records 67 cases (6.7%), notably Brasiléia and Xapuri with 20 each. There are 15 dengue with warning signs; two suspected deaths under investigation. Laboratory confirmation (706, 71.1%) predominates; 286 (28.8%) were confirmed clinically.

article.articleHeadline: Texas Tech researchers secure NIH funding for tropical diseases
article.articleSummary: Texas Tech University researchers Peter Keyel and Kai Zhang secured roughly $600,000 from NIH/NIAID over three years to study leishmaniasis. The disease manifests in cutaneous (most common), mucocutaneous (can cause disability and disfigurement), and visceral forms (untreated fatal in many cases). The project fuses Keyel's work on cell membrane repair with Zhang's parasitology expertise, aiming to identify shared and divergent features between mammalian cells and Leishmania to illuminate fundamental repair mechanisms. Researchers will examine how pore-forming toxins interact with parasite membranes and seek vulnerabilities across Leishmania species. After establishing basic understanding, the team plans translational steps toward inhibitors, followed by efficacy and safety testing, with fall-term undergraduate training to involve students.

article.articleHeadline: How to Prevent Outbreaks of Golden Spot on Coffee
article.articleSummary: Golden spot on coffee, caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. garcae, threatens leaves, branches, and berries. From Sept 2025 to July 2026, risk rises in multiple producing regions due to irregular rainfall, winds, and temperature swings, requiring frequent field monitoring. Symptoms begin as dark, water-soaked spots on young leaves with a yellow halo, progressing to necrotic lesions, leaf drop, and shoot dieback; fruits may show dark spots and abortion of small beans on heavily affected limbs. The bacterium survives on crop residues, diseased plants, and equipment, spreading mainly through rain splash, wind, irrigation water, and handling. Diagnosis relies on field recognition of halos and early lesions, with lab confirmation if uncertain. Management emphasizes prevention: healthy planting material, sanitation, wound-minimizing pruning, residue management, canopy ventilation, appropriate spacing, balanced nutrition, and irrigation; pesticides may be used as advised and per regulations. Ongoing monitoring and technical guidance are essential.

article.articleHeadline: São Bernardo records first death from spotted fever in Greater ABC in 2026.
article.articleSummary: First death from Brazilian spotted fever in Greater ABC in 2026 occurred in São Bernardo. In São Paulo State, 18 confirmed cases this year, with 17 resulting in death; one case recovered. Probable infection sites: Piracicaba (3), Campinas (3), Sorocaba (3), and São José dos Campos (1); others under investigation. Spotted fever is an acute febrile illness caused by Rickettsia and transmitted by ticks such as the star tick and horse tick; transmission is not person-to-person. Early diagnosis is challenging because initial symptoms resemble dengue, influenza, and leptospirosis; from days 2–5, a rash appears on the palms and soles and spreads inward. Exposure history is crucial. Doxycycline, about seven days, is the treatment of choice for suspected cases and may be stopped after 48–72 hours afebrile with medical assessment. Public health measures include mandatory notification, case investigation, epidemiological monitoring, laboratory strengthening, professional training, and cross-sector surveillance to identify risk areas.

article.articleHeadline: Understanding the signs of leprosy and how to prevent it.
article.articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) remains prevalent in North Sulawesi, Indonesia, with 179 new cases reported in the first half of 2026 and 411 cases in 2025. The infection is caused by Mycobacterium leprae and mostly affects the skin and peripheral nerves, but can involve the eyes and upper respiratory tract. Common signs include chronically discolored skin patches (white, red, or brown) that do not heal, numbness or loss of sensation within patches, tingling in hands and feet—especially fingers—enlarged nerves at the elbows, wrists, behind the knees, or neck, and non-healing injuries to hands or feet due to numbness. Additional features include difficulty closing the eyes, thinning eyebrows, and facial changes. Transmission occurs via droplets from an untreated patient during prolonged close contact; however most people have natural resistance, so spread is not as easy as commonly assumed. Early detection and treatment are crucial to prevent disability.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquito Populations Surge During Hot Weather: Know the Disease Risks and the Locations That Become Their Breeding Grounds.
article.articleSummary: Hot weather accelerates mosquito breeding cycles, shortening adult lifespan but speeding development from egg to larva to adult, raising household mosquito populations in tropical areas. Studies cited from the National Library of Medicine on Anopheles gambiae at 27°C, 30°C, and 32°C show that higher temperatures shorten mosquito longevity while hastening physiological development; older mosquitoes at higher temperatures are more prone to death and show higher susceptibility to bacterial infections, with Escherichia coli infection intensity increasing with heat. Mosquitoes are poikilothermic and their metabolism rises with ambient temperature, intensifying growth, survival challenges, and infection responses. The result is a potentially higher risk of malaria and dengue fever outbreaks as populations surge. Breeding sites at home include damp areas from standing water, wet laundry, and poor ventilation, especially in tropical climates.

article.articleHeadline: There are already 4 imported cases in Jingzhou! Urgent reminder.
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-07-21, Jingzhou, China, has reported 4 imported dengue fever cases since May, with infections traced to travelers from Indonesia, Cambodia and Malaysia. Dengue is among the three summer-mosquito transmitted illnesses highlighted in the article, alongside chikungunya and Zika, all spread principally by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Dengue typically presents with abrupt high fever, myalgia, rash and possible bleeding; chikungunya with fever and intense joint pain; Zika often mild but poses pregnancy-related risks. The piece urges preventive measures during hot, humid summer: use repellents, wear protective clothing, sleep under nets with screens, eliminate indoor and outdoor standing water, and prefer air-conditioned accommodations. Post-travel monitoring for 14 days is advised; seek medical care promptly if fever, joint pain, or rash occurs and report travel and exposure history.

article.articleHeadline: Fresh diarrhoea outbreak in city, 14 hospitalised
article.articleSummary: Diarrhoeal outbreak in Giripuram, Vijayawada, hospitalising 14 residents from two lanes on July 18 after vomiting and loose motions. Cases confined to two lanes serving about 850 residents; Giripuram overall has roughly 3,000. The Vijayawada Municipal Corporation (VMC) and Health Department intensified surveillance with door-to-door checks, water-quality testing, and sample collection. Preliminary results showed no contamination and satisfactory residual chlorine; samples have been sent to the Institute of Preventive Medicine (IPM), Guntur for detailed analysis, with reports due on Sunday. All patients are stable; only a few remain under observation. Authorities are inspecting private RO water plants for compliance with testing and record-keeping, and will act on irregularities. The incident follows a major outbreak in New Rajarajeshwari Rao Pet months earlier, where 275 recovered and 42 remained under treatment before containment.

The district records about 160 TB deaths annually and currently around 5,000 patients are on TB therapy. Free drugs are available at government and private centers; government hospitals offer free TB treatment. Symptoms include persistent cough, coughing up blood, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue; two-week persistent cough warrants immediate testing. TB is airborne; contacts should be tested. The campaign includes free testing, medications, counseling, nutrition support, and an ASHA worker incentive of Rs 500 per identified positive case.

article.articleHeadline: ETV Bharat's Monsoon Manual Provides A State-By-State Report On The Rainy Season's Biggest Health Risks, Outbreaks And Prevention
article.articleSummary: India faces a rising monsoon health risk as climate change disrupts rainfall and expands dengue across states such as Assam, Kerala, Delhi, and Tamil Nadu, per ETV Bharat's nationwide series (published 20 July 2026). Five-year state-wise data show dengue surging while malaria and kala-azar decline due to sustained interventions. Heavy rains and floods create stagnant water that breeds mosquitoes and contaminate drinking water with sewage, fueling typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A, leptospirosis, and acute diarrhoeal illnesses. Intermittent downpours and floods complicate prediction of outbreaks, with non-communicable diseases like diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease worsening outcomes in infected individuals. Young children under five bear the highest burden, with diarrhoea, pneumonia, and mosquito-borne illnesses driving hospitalisations; vaccination and adequate nutrition remain key defenses. The state-by-state approach highlights local risk profiles across Assam, Delhi, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and beyond.

article.articleHeadline: Mixed malaria spreading in Bastar, 8,426 people infected; learn the symptoms and ways to prevent.
article.articleSummary: Mixed malaria outbreak in Bastar division, Chhattisgarh, with 8,426 malaria cases since January 2026, including 254 mixed infections of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. Over 663,000 blood samples have been tested. District counts: Bijapur 3,173; Sukma 1,686; Dantewada 1,344; Narayanpur 896; Bastar 809; Kondagaon 329; Kanker 189. Mixed malaria occurs when both parasite species are transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, and is considered more dangerous due to potential severe complications affecting brain, kidneys, and liver. Common symptoms include high fever, chills, headache, vomiting, fatigue, and anemia, with fever potentially recurring. Preventive measures urged: eliminate standing water around homes, use bed nets regularly, and seek timely diagnosis and treatment for fever to curb spread. (Date reference: 2026-07-20.)

article.articleHeadline: Viatris launches support project in Maharashtra to combat DR-TB

Key activities include processing more than 26,000 samples across four Nagpur locations, household tracing of confirmed TB and DR-TB cases targeting 22,000 households, and distribution of more than 450 nutrition kits to TB/DR-TB patients. Since 2020, Viatris has screened over 1.5 million people for TB in India and supported 58,000 people in Gadchiroli district, Maharashtra. Globally, Viatris has helped enable DR-TB treatment access for over 300,000 patients.

article.articleHeadline: Research advances offer hope, but prevention remains key in Rabies control: AIIMS Neurologist
article.articleSummary: Darbhanga, 20 Jul — Rabies remains almost 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear; prevention via timely post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is the only proven life-saving strategy, AIIMS neurologist Prof (Dr) Achal Kumar Srivastava told the 26th National Conference of APCRI in Darbhanga. While highlighting research advances—monoclonal antibodies, gene therapy, next-generation mRNA vaccines, and advanced molecular diagnostics—he cautioned that these will require extensive trials before clinical adoption. Global estimates from WHO: about 59,000 rabies deaths annually, ~95% in Asia and Africa; children under 15 account for ~40%. The rabies virus travels to the brain via peripheral nerves; two clinical forms: furious and paralytic. Encouraging preclinical results for F11 monoclonal antibody; other therapies under study. Milwaukee Protocol not reliably effective. Current management focuses on intensive supportive care; real-time RT-PCR and LAMP improve early diagnosis. One Health: dog vaccination, public awareness, timely PEP, and cross-sector coordination are essential.

article.articleHeadline: After a vacation, a shocking discovery awaited her: 38 parasites were found in her brain.
article.articleSummary: Neurocysticercosis caused by Taenia solium larvae was diagnosed in Lowri Denman after a 2007 three‑month trip to India. An MRI revealed 38 brain cysts; initial suspicion of toxoplasmosis was ruled out. Transmission occurs from ingesting eggs in contaminated water or food, not pork, with hygiene gaps increasing risk. Neurocysticercosis is a common cause of acquired epilepsy in developing regions of Latin America, Africa, and Asia; in the UK and most of Europe it remains rare and usually travel- or immigrant‑associated. After a two‑week hospitalization, antiparasitic therapy with steroids reduced inflammation, but later cerebral swelling and neuropsychiatric symptoms required six weeks in a neuropsychiatric unit. The parasites died and calcified, leaving a lifelong need for antiepileptic treatment. Clinicians in Britain and the US deem this a rare, travel‑linked case, underscoring the importance of food and water safety and hygiene for travelers.

article.articleHeadline: Assam: Tinsukia imposes 30-day pork trade ban after ASF outbreak
article.articleSummary: As of 20 July 2026, Assam’s Tinsukia district imposes a 30-day pork trade ban after an African Swine Fever (ASF) outbreak centered in Simoluguri village, Kailashpur Gaon Panchayat, Margherita. A 1-km infected zone and 10-km surveillance zone are established; all pork shops in Digboi Co-District are closed for 30 days. Sale, transport and movement of pigs and pork products within and outside the co-district, including to Arunachal Pradesh, are prohibited. A culling operation will run July 21–23, with veterinary teams overseeing culling, carcass disposal, sanitisation and biosecurity measures per ASF guidelines. This is the second ASF outbreak in Tinsukia within six weeks; a June 9 outbreak at Ouguri village, Rupai Siding, Doomdooma Block prompted culling and containment. ASF has killed more than 40,000 pigs, affecting over 14,000 pig-rearing families across 22 districts, with up to 100% fatality. The Disaster Management Act 2005 order may invoke BNS Section 223.

article.articleHeadline: Monsoon fuels rise in flu cases; Karnataka health department strengthens surveillance
article.articleSummary: Seasonal influenza in Karnataka, India, is rising with 2,056 laboratory-confirmed cases from January to the second week of July 2026. Monthly counts climbed from 242 in April to 383 in May and 414 in June, the year’s highest totals; by the second week of July, 324 cases had been recorded in July so far, versus 383 for all of July 2025, signaling a sharper monsoon build-up. Karnataka typically has two seasonal peaks—January–March and July–September—and officials attribute the spike to weather patterns. The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) directs districts to strengthen surveillance, ensure sample collection and laboratory consumables, and maintain stocks of Oseltamivir, PPE, and N95 masks. Hospitals should keep ventilators ready, and public campaigns should emphasize cough etiquette, hand hygiene, mask use, and seeking early care. Minister UT Khader chaired the review; Ritvik Ranjanam Pandey commented on preparedness.

article.articleHeadline: During the monsoon, a little negligence can be life-threatening: measures to protect cows and buffaloes from diseases.
article.articleSummary: As of July 21, 2026, in Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh, India, the monsoon raises disease risk for cows and buffaloes. Mastitis (thunela) spreads rapidly; after milking, keep animals off damp floors and clean the teats. Vaccinate on schedule against Foot-and-Mouth Disease (khurpka-muhpaka) and galghontu (throat infection). Humidity, mud, and filth increase pneumonia, diarrhea, fever, skin infections, and calf illnesses, with newborns most vulnerable; seek veterinary guidance promptly. Dr. Hemant Shah emphasizes dry, clean, ventilated shelters; if an animal gets drenched, move it to a dry area. Calves require colostrum within an hour of birth. Feeding should avoid spoiled fodder; mix green fodder with dry hay to aid digestion. Mosquitoes, flies and parasites proliferate in rain, so prevent water stagnation and maintain hygiene, using medicines as needed.

article.articleHeadline: Holiday hotspots where four rare diseases cause joint pains and bleeding gums
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya, dengue, schistosomiasis and Lyme disease are highlighted as travel-related risks for Britons this summer. Chikungunya is spread by daytime-biting Aedes mosquitoes and is found in over 120 countries from the Caribbean to Sri Lanka and Thailand; UK travellers returning with it are up about 43%. Dengue, also carried by Aedes, affects India, Barbados, Thailand and parts of the Americas and southern Europe, including France, Italy and Spain; symptoms typically start 4–10 days after a bite and include fever, headache, rash, and muscle or joint pain, with severe forms causing bleeding gums, vomiting or breathing problems. Schistosomiasis, caused by parasitic worms in freshwater, occurs in Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, with 200 million cases worldwide; Europe has seen Corsica and Spain outbreaks. Lyme disease, tick-borne bacterial infection, is present in Europe, North America and Asia; about 10% of UK ticks carry it, with a 20% yearly increase. Prevention: cover up, use mosquito nets and repellents; avoid freshwater swimming and seek care if symptoms appear.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-19 Cases Continue to Rise Across Thailand with 6633 New Confirmed Cases and 257 Hospitalizations in the Last 7 Days
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 infections continue to rise in Thailand. Week 29 (July 13–19, 2026) recorded 6,633 laboratory-confirmed cases and 257 hospitalizations nationwide, indicating active circulation. Despite official figures, experts warn true infections may be substantially higher due to reduced testing in hospitals and clinics, especially for mild respiratory symptoms. NB.1.8.1 remains the dominant SARS‑CoV‑2 lineage in Thailand; no evidence of increased severity versus prior variants. Genomic surveillance is limited, and officials monitor for emerging RF.5 sub-lineages associated with higher severity in Andhra Pradesh, India, but their presence in Thailand is not confirmed. The Department of Disease Control reports no COVID‑19 deaths in the latest period, though some clinicians note unexplained deaths and occasional organ failure; investigations are ongoing. Public health emphasis remains on expanding testing, strengthening genomic surveillance, transparent reporting, and investigating unusual severe illnesses to identify new threats.

article.articleHeadline: Warning! A 37-year-old Thai man infected with mpox (Mpox) Clade 1b; Dr. Manoon reveals the initial symptoms and treatment.
article.articleSummary: On 21 July 2026, a 37-year-old Thai man with HIV on long-term antiretroviral therapy and a history of syphilis presented to Vichaiyut Hospital in Bangkok with fever, rigors, myalgia and fatigue for three days, followed by widespread small pustules on the face, trunk, limbs, genitals, and perianal area; eyes and mouth mucosa were spared. He reported sex with a foreign male partner about one month earlier. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted; no fever at examination. PCR of vesicular fluid and the upper lesion skin confirmed Monkeypox (Mpox) Clade 1b. Diagnosis: Mpox Clade 1b with HIV infection. Treatment: Tecovirimat given twice daily for 14 days; the patient tolerated therapy and lesions decreased. He was advised home isolation for three weeks until crusts healed and new skin covered the previous lesions to prevent transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Half of approved diagnostics for Africa's priority epidemic diseases unavailable at primary healthcare level - Report
article.articleSummary: Half of approved diagnostics for six Africa CDC priority diseases—Mpox, dengue, cholera, bacterial meningitis, malaria and Ebola—cannot be used at primary healthcare centres because they require laboratory infrastructure beyond frontline facilities. Ebola diagnostics are the most laboratory-dependent, with 88% needing a lab; across the six diseases, 577 diagnostics exist with 288 requiring clinical lab infrastructure and 59 still under development. Malaria has 83% deployable at primary care, but most Ebola and Mpox tests remain lab-based. Funding for diagnostic R&D has declined since 2015, from about $55 million to under $26 million in 2024, a nearly $4 million annual drop, signaling underinvestment amid rising outbreak risk. The Diagnostics Deficit report, by PATH and Impact Global Health, launched ahead of the AU Extraordinary Health Summit in Accra, Ghana, warns of gaps in access, affordability, deployment, and manufacturing readiness. The 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak highlighted detection delays due to strain-mismatch tests, underscoring urgent needs.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia Launches Final Round of Polio Vaccination Campaign Targeting 3.9 Million Children
article.articleSummary: Polio vaccination campaign underway in Zambia's six priority provinces (Lusaka, Southern, Eastern, Central, Western, Muchinga), targeting about 3.9 million children under five as the final round of Sub-National Immunization Activities runs 21–26 July 2026. This follows two earlier rounds in April and June as part of regional outbreak response, boosted by a newly solarized 100-kW National Vaccine Store to strengthen the vaccine cold chain; projected annual savings ~$48,000. Across rounds, 6 provinces, 71 districts, 1,985 facilities with 7,830 vaccination teams and 8,006 mobilizers/supervisors participated. Round 1 reached 3,841,940 (102% of 3,759,057 target); Round 2 3,979,228 (103% of 3,845,667). Zero-dose children declined from 1.5% to 0.55%. The campaign, supported by GPEI, WHO, Rotary, UNICEF, KSRelief, UAE, aims to interrupt poliovirus transmission after environmental detections in Lusaka earlier this year. Final doses cover children who received prior doses; all under-five children offered oral polio vaccine at diverse venues.

article.articleHeadline: Fox killed after latest local rabies scare
article.articleSummary: Mechanicville, NY — A fox suspected of biting a resident and charging others was killed by police Monday; the carcass was turned over to the state DEC for rabies testing. The animal had an unsteady gait and appeared aggressive. The bite victim, a woman on Elizabeth Street, was hospitalized. A separate incident on North Seventh Avenue saw the same fox charge at a man and his two children before it was captured. Rabies testing had not yet been completed, but officials expected swift results. The episode adds to ongoing rabies concerns in the Capital Region, with beavers suspected of rabies attacking bathers at Turtle Island, Lake George (July 9), a rabid horse near Fultonville, and a rabies-positive skunk on Swan Street, Amsterdam.
